interest: This file offers valuable insight into the immediate administrative and legal friction between the United States, Great Britain, and Japan following the outbreak of hostilities in December 1941, specifically regarding the dual use and legal designation of passenger liners as hospital ships versus diplomatic repatriation vessels. It illustrates the State Department's practical dilemma in early 1942 over whether designating exchange ships as hospital ships might lead to fatal military misunderstandings or legal violations, prompting U.S. planners to borrow German precedent by affixing prominent 'DIPLOMAT' markings and illuminated national insignia. Furthermore, the extensive Treaty Division study by Charles I. Bevans provides historians with a definitive contemporary snapshot of how the United States government interpreted the complex web of multilateral treaties on the laws of war, capturing the exact diplomatic cables via Switzerland through which Japan agreed to adhere to the 1929 Geneva conventions on a reciprocal, mutatis mutandis basis.
overview: File 894.241/1 (File 1326) concerns Japanese hospital ships, transport vessel markings, and the international legal conventions governing naval and land warfare at the outbreak of the Pacific War in early 1942. The file originates from a January 28, 1942 inquiry by the U.S. Navy Department transmitting a British Admiralty message regarding Japan's notification that three merchant vessels—the Hikawa Maru, Takasago Maru, and Asahi Maru—would be employed as hospital ships under the Geneva Convention. In interdepartmental correspondence between the Special Division, the Liaison Office, and the Navy Department, U.S. officials coordinate a response to a Japanese proposal conveyed via the Spanish Embassy to utilize these ships for the mutual exchange of diplomatic and civilian personnel, debating whether they should be marked as hospital ships or given distinct 'Diplomat' markings. Accompanying this correspondence is an extensive 27-page reference memorandum prepared by Charles I. Bevans of the State Department's Treaty Division (revised March 28, 1942), compiling the ratifications, adherences, reservations, and diplomatic notes concerning the Hague and Geneva Conventions of 1864, 1899, 1904, 1906, 1907, and 1929, including Japan's wartime commitment to observe the 1929 Geneva Red Cross Convention and apply the 1929 Prisoners of War Convention mutatis mutandis.

subfiles.about: Transmits British Admiralty intelligence concerning Japan's notification of three hospital ships and inquires whether the U.S. received similar notice.
subfiles.from: Captain R. E. Schuirmann, U.S.N. (Navy Department)
subfiles.summary: Captain Schuirmann informs the Secretary of State of a message from the British Admiralty reporting that Japan has notified under the Geneva Convention that the Hikawa Maru, Takasago Maru, and Asahi Maru (spelled Asami Maru) will be employed as hospital ships. The message details the ships' physical dimensions, white hull paint, electrically illuminated red crosses, and distinctive funnel markings, adding that an Admiralty Fleet Order will accept them as hospital ships. Schuirmann requests clarification as to whether Japan has notified the United States of any hospital ships under Hague Convention X of 1907 and asks for copies of any relevant notes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Captain R. E. Schuirmann (Navy Department) to Secretary of State on Japanese Hospital Ships

subfiles.about: Discusses proposed markings for Japanese diplomatic exchange vessels to avoid confusing them with hospital ships.
subfiles.summary: The Special Division writes to Stephen Morris noting that a draft reply to the Japanese proposal regarding exchange vessels is being submitted to Assistant Secretary Breckinridge Long. The division recommends that the exchange ships not be marked as hospital ships to prevent misunderstanding, suggesting instead markings adapted from German ideas: white hulls, national flags, vessel and country names, and the word 'DIPLOMAT', with full illumination at night. Morris is asked to obtain any recommendations or improvements on these proposed markings from the Navy Department.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Special Division to S. Morris on Diplomatic Exchange Ship Markings

subfiles.about: Transmits Captain Schuirmann's letter on hospital ships and acknowledges the Spanish Embassy memorandum regarding personnel exchange.
subfiles.summary: Stephen Morris of the Under Secretary's Liaison Office thanks Albert E. Clattenburg for providing a copy of the Spanish Embassy's memorandum of January 6 concerning Japan's proposal to exchange Japanese and American personnel. Morris confirms that he forwarded that memorandum to Captain Schuirmann of the Navy Department, highlighting paragraph 6. In turn, Morris transmits Captain Schuirmann's letter containing the British Admiralty message regarding Japanese hospital ships.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from S. Morris to Albert E. Clattenburg regarding Spanish Embassy Memorandum and British Admiralty Message

subfiles.about: A dated carbon copy of the Liaison Office memorandum concerning personnel exchange and the Admiralty hospital ship message.
subfiles.summary: This document is a dated copy (January 28, 1942) of Stephen Morris's memorandum to Albert E. Clattenburg. It records the transmission to Captain Schuirmann of the Spanish Embassy's January 6 memorandum concerning the proposal for the exchange of American and Japanese personnel, drawing specific attention to paragraph 6. It also encloses Captain Schuirmann's letter communicating the British Admiralty's notification of Japanese hospital ships.
subfiles.title: Duplicate Memorandum from S. Morris to Albert E. Clattenburg on Japanese Personnel Exchange and Hospital Ships

subfiles.about: Replies to the Navy Department regarding Japanese exchange vessels, enclosing the Spanish Embassy note and requesting suggestions on ship markings.
subfiles.from: Orme Wilson (Liaison Officer, Department of State)
subfiles.summary: Orme Wilson replies to the Navy Department's inquiry concerning the British Admiralty message about the Hikawa Maru, Takasago Maru, and Asahi Maru. Wilson encloses the Spanish Embassy's January 6 memorandum containing Japan's proposal for the exchange of Japanese and American personnel, noting that paragraph 6 represents all the information State has received on these ships. He explains that State is considering a draft reply proposing that the vessels not be marked as hospital ships, but rather display white hulls, national flags, ship and country names, and the word 'Diplomat' with night lighting, and requests Navy suggestions on improving these markings.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Orme Wilson to Director of Central Division, Navy Department, on Markings for Japanese Exchange Vessels

subfiles.about: Surveys ratifications, adherences, reservations, and wartime status of the Hague and Geneva Conventions on land and naval warfare.
subfiles.from: Charles I. Bevans (Treaty Division, Department of State)
subfiles.summary: Prepared by Charles I. Bevans of the Treaty Division and revised as of March 28, 1942, this 27-page memorandum provides an exhaustive legal compilation of the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907, the Geneva Red Cross Conventions of 1864, 1906, and 1929, the 1904 Hague Hospital Ships Convention, and the 1929 Geneva Prisoners of War Convention. It enumerates the ratifications, adherences, reservations, and general participation clauses for each treaty to determine binding obligations among World War II belligerents and neutrals. The document concludes by quoting State Department and Swiss Legation telegrams from December 1941 and February 1942 confirming that Japan agreed to strictly observe the Geneva Red Cross Convention and apply the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention mutatis mutandis to American POWs.
subfiles.title: Treaty Division Memorandum on Hague and Geneva Conventions Governing Land and Naval Warfare
